extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners, patent practitioners, and patent litigators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating obviousness under 35 U.S.C. § 103, with emphasis on chemical/pharmaceutical lead-compound cases and several rationales for obviousness (use of known technique, predictable results, obvious-to-try). Explains required factual findings, examples, and how to treat secondary considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead compound/structural similarity as basis for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness based on structural similarity can be proven by identification of some motivation that would have led one of ordinary skill in the art to select and then modify a known compound (a lead compound) in a particular way to achieve the claimed compound; an expectation of similar properties in light of the prior art can be sufficient even without an explicit teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The requisite motivation can come from any number of sources and need not be explicit in the art. Structural similarity may create an expectation that the new compound will have 'similar properties' to the old in light of the totality of the prior art (Eisai, Aventis). Office personnel should look for a reason to select and modify the prior art compound; explicit motivation in the reference is not required, but there must be some articulable reason to start with that compound other than its mere existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual meaning and selection of 'lead compound'
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'lead compound' may have a contextual legal meaning different from how pharmaceutical chemists use it; any known compound might serve as a lead compound for an obviousness analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A compound that is inactive or that a chemist would not select for business/practical reasons could still be used as a lead for an obviousness rejection if there is a reason (other than mere existence) to select and modify it. However, there must be some articulated reason to begin with that particular lead compound (Altana, Eisai, Ortho-McNeil, Altana/Teva cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a reason to select and modify a lead compound
rubrics_metrics.description: To support an obviousness rejection based on a lead compound, there must be some reason for selecting that particular compound and for modifying it to arrive at the claimed compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reason need not be explicitly stated in the prior art but must be articulable from the totality of the prior art, common knowledge, or other sources. Mere structural similarity or existence of the compound is insufficient without a reason to select and modify (Altana Pharma AG v. Teva; Eisai; Ortho-McNeil).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness without identifying a single lead compound
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed chemical compound may be obvious even without identifying a single lead compound if the prior art suggests formulating a compound having certain structurally defined moieties or moieties with certain properties, and one of ordinary skill would have known how to synthesize such a compound and predict the structural/functional result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: when a claim can be viewed as two known compounds linked by a chemical linker, an obviousness finding may be proper if there is a reason to link them, a person of ordinary skill knows how to do so, and the resulting compound would have been a predictable result of the linkage. Office personnel should consider teachings that suggest classes of moieties or linking strategies, not only single lead compounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of secondary considerations (unexpected results, commercial success, long-felt need)
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary considerations (objective indicia) can rebut a prima facie case of obviousness; unexpected results, commercial success, and evidence of satisfying a long-felt but unsolved need are relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexpected superior properties (e.g., potency, toxicity profile) presented with credible evidence and witness testimony can rebut obviousness (Procter & Gamble v. Teva). Commercial success is probative but may be given less weight if competing products are assigned to the same party. Long-felt need should be evaluated as of the filing date, not market date. Office personnel should analyze such evidence in detail when presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: Use of known technique to improve similar devices (methods or products) — required findings
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim on the ground of applying a known technique to improve similar devices/methods/products, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and articulate specific findings: (1) prior art contained a 'base' device; (2) prior art contained a 'comparable' device that has been improved in the same way; (3) one of ordinary skill could have applied the known improvement technique to the base device and the results would have been predictable; and (4) any additional Graham-based findings necessary to explain obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rationale rests on the proposition that an enhancement technique recognized in other situations becomes part of the ordinary capabilities of one skilled in the art. If any of the findings cannot be made, this rationale cannot support an obviousness conclusion. See examples such as Intel v. PACT XPP and Nilssen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: Applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement — required findings
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim where a known technique is applied to a known device that was 'ready for improvement', Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and articulate: (1) the prior art contained a 'base' device; (2) the prior art contained a known technique applicable to the base device; (3) one of ordinary skill would have recognized that applying the known technique would have yielded predictable results and an improved system; and (4) any other Graham-based findings necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rationale emphasizes that the technique must be within ordinary capabilities and the device must be ready for improvement with predictable results. Examples include Dann v. Johnston and In re Nilssen. If predictability or applicability cannot be established, this rationale fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious-to-try rationale — required findings
rubrics_metrics.description: To rely on an 'obvious to try' rationale, Office personnel must resolve Graham factual inquiries and articulate: (1) there was a recognized problem or need in the art at the relevant time; (2) there was a finite number of identified, predictable potential solutions; (3) one of ordinary skill could have pursued the known potential solutions with a reasonable expectation of success; and (4) any additional Graham-based findings necessary to explain obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR teaches that when there are a finite number of identified, predictable solutions and a reasonable expectation of success, pursuing those options may show the product of ordinary skill rather than innovation. However, courts emphasize predictability and expect courts/examiners to consider the state of the science/technology, specificity of prior art, and predictability of results (Pfizer v. Apotex; Alza; Kubin). The 'finite number' requirement and reasonable expectation of success are critical; mere hindsight is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability and reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable expectation of success and predictability of results are required for several obviousness rationales (lead-compound modifications, applying known techniques, obvious-to-try).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts place particular emphasis on predictability in the chemical and biotech arts. Lack of evidence that modifications would have been routine, unpredictable results, or demonstrated unpredictability in the art can defeat obviousness (Procter & Gamble, In re Kubin, In re Urbanski). Examiners should evaluate whether necessary modifications were routine and whether the skilled artisan would have had a reasonable expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples as evidentiary guidance (Aventis, Eisai, Procter & Gamble, Altana, Pfizer, Alza, Kubin, Urbanski)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use judicial examples to inform factual findings — e.g., Aventis (5(S) ramipril) — expectation of similar properties and structural similarity; Eisai — structural similarity and expectation of similar properties but lack of reason to modify can defeat obviousness; Procter & Gamble — unexpected results and secondary considerations rebut obviousness; Altana — multiple compounds can be natural choices and restrictive 'single-lead' view is improper; Pfizer/Alza/Kubin/Urbanski illustrate obvious-to-try and predictability analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel should rely on the case law to assess which factual predicates were dispositive (motivation to modify, predictability, routine nature of modifications, evidence of unexpected results). The MPEP supplies the examples to illustrate how to weigh and articulate the necessary findings.
